headline: Week: views 17,289→18,344 (+1,055), subs 24→25 (+1 — again). Ep 10 went live 8/14 and YouTube handed it the biggest launch-day audition in channel history (3,597 impressions in roughly the first day of reach coverage; Ep 9 needed a week to reach 2,527) — and it converted at 0.61% CTR, the worst episode CTR ever, below even solo Ep 7's 0.68%. Compounding it: the live title ('Gorilla Mode: How AI Swarms Change Everything') matches NONE of the four drafts in segment-times.md, which records draft #1 as published and yt_fetch-verified on 8/14 — so a retitle or an unlogged Test & Compare happened mid-launch, exactly the failure mode the packaging gate exists to catch. The ≤60s cold-open experiment read negative: Ep 10 lost −69.6pp by 1:42 (Ep 9: −58.7pp), so brevity alone doesn't stop the leak (n=23, noisy). The genuinely new win: the perp-rides-all-episode format produced the strongest ending on the channel — watch RISES from 8.7% to 13% at 82–97% with vs_typical 0.91+. And the funnel verdict is in: RELATED_VIDEO moved 130→150 views in a week while shorts added ~1,850 — still flat, so clip picks pivot to arc-teases on Ep 11.

production.title: Ep 10 launch packaging FAILED the gate: 0.61% CTR on the biggest launch audition ever, and the serving title is undocumented
production.evidence: Reach coverage through 8/15 07:00Z (≈ launch day + a few hours): 3,597 impressions at 0.61% CTR. Targets from the 8/10 review: Ep 6's 3.24%; even Ep 8's 1.78% and Ep 9's 1.23% are 2–3× better. ~95% of lifetime impressions land in the first 7 days, so this is the window that matters. Separately, the API now returns the title 'Gorilla Mode: How AI Swarms Change Everything' — not draft #1 ('The Agents Built Their Own 4chan…') which segment-times.md records as published and yt_fetch-verified 8/14, and not any of the other three drafts. Ep 9's truncated-variant fiasco started the same way.
production.recommendation: Ep 10 is only 3 days into its 7-day window — a packaging fix can still run, unlike every retro-fix before it. Jackson: confirm in Studio what's actually serving (retitle? Test & Compare? which thumbnail?), pick the strongest verified title+thumbnail now, then backfill segment-times.md (house rule: it reflects the ACTUAL live copy). Going forward the gate gains a line: any post-publish title/thumbnail change gets logged in segment-times.md same day.

production.title: Cold-open cap shipped on Ep 10 — the leak didn't move; next edit-side lever is a ONE-beat open
production.evidence: Ep 10 shipped the ≤60s cap (51.5s, three chained beats with whoosh+wipe between). Result: 100% watching at 0:34 → 52.2% at 1:08 → 30.4% at 1:42, a −69.6pp loss vs Ep 9's −58.7pp over the same span (caveat: n=23 measured views, each viewer ≈ 4.3pp). The drop concentrates at 0:34–1:08 — beats 2–3 of the teaser plus the title card, before the perp even starts at 1:46. Low-intent browse traffic from the huge audition likely inflates this, but two episodes running the leak is inside the teaser itself.
production.recommendation: Ep 11: cut the cold open to ONE beat — the single strongest moment, ~20–25s, straight into the title card. Stop chaining teasers; each extra beat is another exit ramp. Keep the ≤60s hard cap as a ceiling, not a target.
production.status_note: Cap itself: shipped and verified on Ep 10 (51.5s). The metric it was meant to fix: unmoved.

recording.title: Stakes that ride the whole episode produce the channel's best ending — make the live-resolution finale a format staple
recording.evidence: Ep 10's perp (long PUMP 10×) opened at 1:46, rode as a corner pip all episode, resolved at the wrap. The back fifth is the strongest ending ever recorded: watch RISES 8.7%→13.0% from 77% to 82% and holds 13% through 97% (46:39–55:11, Boltz → Ethereum → wrap), with vs_typical 0.91–0.92 — triple the mid-show relative performance. Ep 9's best-on-channel body ended at 9.8%. Survivors don't drift off; they stay for the resolution.
recording.recommendation: Every episode carries one live, unresolved stake introduced in the first 5 minutes and resolved in the wrap (Perp of Fortune already is this — keep it, and tease the resolution in the cold open). This also confirms the 8/10 finding: end on the live/personal beat, never park a standing topic in the last 20%.

recording.title: Story explainers hold, but only to the payoff — Chris's Friday-night swarm leaked its back half
recording.evidence: Ep 10's Black Hat swarm story (5:55–14:24) held and even climbed (13.0% at 9:40 → 21.7–26.1% around 10:48–11:22 as replays/chapter entries land). Then 'Chris's Friday-night swarm' (14:24–21:31, ~7 min): watch halves 17.4%→8.7% across 14:47–15:55 and vs_typical craters 0.55→0.21 by 18:12 — the last leak of the episode; the curve never drops again after it. This refines the 8/10 rule: an owner-with-a-story earns the long block (Ep 9's Coldcard, Ep 10's Black Hat story), but a personal PROJECT retelling decays once the demo's punchline lands (n=23 caveat applies).
recording.recommendation: Personal-project segments end at the payoff: land the punchline, tease what's next, move on — ~4 min, not 7. Owner-story explainers keep the 12-min license.

recording.title: Don't ship a solo episode as the main feed item (standing)
recording.evidence: Unchanged since 7/31: Ep 7 (solo) remains worst on every axis except Ep 10's launch CTR — 0.68% CTR, 6.8% avg view, −56.7pp opening. All full-panel episodes since beat it on avg view %.
recording.recommendation: When hosts are out, ship a clip package or bring a guest.
